questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [mid] invites, roles and guest access: who may do what once a user is signed in (tracer, docs/adr/0003-sessions-over-jwt.md). Scenario: the issue tracker is sold to agencies. About 120 agency workspaces each have 20 to 60 staff plus 5 to 15 client guests who may see only the one or two teams working on their project; agency admins send about 300 invites a week; when a client contract ends, that client's access must be gone the same day; and an auditor may ask who could see a given team on a given date. Before you look, design the role model, where each permission check runs and what a refusal looks like, how a request for an object by id is authorised, how invites work as credentials, how a role change or removal takes effect, and what you record for the auditor. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Authorisation is one pure decision over the membership: its role plus, for a guest, the list of team ids granted. Admins and members see every team in their workspace, a guest only the listed teams, and because the rule is a plain function the whole role matrix is unit-tested without a database.

[w3] A request for an object by id loads the object first and then runs the gate for the team that object belongs to, so an id guessed or copied from another team gets the same answer as an id that does not exist.

[w2] Refusals collapse to 404 wherever the existence of a workspace or team is itself information, and 403 is kept for callers who already know the thing exists, such as a non-admin in their own workspace attempting an admin action.

[w3] Nothing about roles travels with the session: a session resolves to a user and nothing more, and the team gate reads the membership afresh on every request. A demotion or a removal therefore applies to the very next HTTP request, without touching anyone's session.
[w3] An invite is a credential and gets the same rules as a session token: a random value of which only the hash is stored, a 7-day expiry, and single use, recorded by stamping when it was accepted.

[w2] Guests need a way to be granted teams: accepting any invite creates the membership with an empty team list, and no route changes a role, edits a guest's teams or removes a member, so the design adds admin-only member management (change role, grant or revoke a team, remove).

[w2] Writes need their own rule, not just reads: inside a granted team the team gate is the only check, so a client guest can delete or reassign issues exactly as staff can. Decide which actions a guest may take and check the action, not only the team.

[w1] Answering 'who could see this team on that date' needs a history of grants and revocations: a membership row records only when it was created, so its past roles and team lists are overwritten and lost.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the first month with agencies: an agency admin pastes an invite link into a channel shared with the client; the API's standard output is shipped to a third-party log service; two people at the client click the same link within the same second; a penetration tester reports signing in to production without any GitHub account; a contractor whose membership row was deleted by hand still sees issue titles in My Issues; and an agency member assigns an issue to a user id copied from another workspace. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The pasted link works for whoever clicks it first: accepting checks only that the token exists, has not expired and has not been used, then gives the signed-in user a membership with the invite's role, and the address the invite was sent to is never compared with the account accepting it. Bind acceptance to the invited, verified address, or route it through an admin's approval.

[w3] Hashing the invite at rest is undone by the log line: until email delivery exists, the create handler prints the full invite URL, raw token included, to standard output, so anyone with access to the log service can join any workspace that sent an invite. Deliver the token only to the invitee and never write a credential to a log.

[w2] Both clicks succeed: the used-or-not check reads the invite before the transaction starts, and the update that marks it used does not require it to still be unused, so two concurrent accepts both pass and both create a membership. Make the claim itself conditional (only an unused invite may be marked, exactly one row must change) inside the transaction.

[w3] The fake identity provider ships to production: its routes are registered unconditionally and any provider name other than a fully configured github falls back to the dev provider, so a dev login followed by a callback carrying a code of the form dev:<any name> creates a session for an invented user; the dev authorize route will also redirect to any URL it is handed. Register the dev routes only outside production.

[w2] My Issues lists every issue assigned to the user across every team and workspace, filtered only by assignee and not by current access, so removing a membership does not hide those titles. Every read path filters by access as it stands now, and offboarding also unassigns.

[w3] The update route accepts any user id as the assignee, with no check that this user can see the team, so an outsider can be made assignee: the issue then shows up in that outsider's My Issues, and everyone viewing the team receives the outsider's name and email in the issue payload. Validate the assignee against the same team gate before writing.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your access design against the alternatives: answering 404 versus 403 when a check fails; invite links that work as bearer tokens versus invites bound to an address versus admin approval; reading the role on every request versus carrying it in the session or a token; a guest's teams as an array on the membership versus a join table; three fixed roles versus configurable permissions; and ending a contractor's access by deleting sessions versus removing the membership. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A uniform 404 hides from guests and outsiders that a workspace or team exists at all, at the cost of a harder support conversation ('missing, or not allowed?') and of permission bugs that look like missing data; a 403 is clearer wherever the caller already knows the resource exists.

[w3] Bearer invite links are frictionless and can be forwarded to the right colleague, which is exactly what makes them dangerous; binding them to an address stops forwarding but fails whenever the GitHub account reports a different address or none (the login then falls back to a noreply address); admin approval is the safest and the slowest.

[w2] Reading the membership on every request costs a team lookup and a membership lookup after the session lookup, and buys revocation that is immediate; carrying the role in the session or a token saves those queries and stays wrong until the user signs in again.

[w2] An array of team ids is one row to read and simple to write, but no foreign key protects it (a deleted team leaves a dangling id), nothing indexes 'who can see this team', and computing a user's visible teams means looping over memberships and loading every team of each workspace; a join table costs a join and buys integrity, reverse lookups and a natural place for history.

[w2] Three fixed roles keep the matrix small enough to test exhaustively; agencies will soon ask for a read-only client or a guest who may comment but not edit, and configurable permissions cover that at the cost of a matrix nobody can review at a glance.

[w2] Sessions belong to the user, not to a workspace: a contractor removed from one agency may still work for another, so deleting their sessions would sign them out everywhere, while removing the one membership ends exactly the access that the contract covered.

[w1] A convenience meant for local development and CI belongs behind the environment check made at boot, because the decision record assumes the dev provider never runs in production and nothing in the code enforces it.
keyPoints.quote: Users authenticate via OAuth (a dev provider locally/CI, GitHub in prod).
